tagline: CC: security principles, access control, incident response

scenarios.title: The clinic's three promises
scenarios.situation: A small clinic asks you what information security means for their patient records. The manager wants one plain-language explanation they can share with staff.
scenarios.prompt: Which explanation correctly maps the CIA triad?
choices: Confidentiality means the records are backed up, integrity means they are encrypted, availability means everyone can see them
Confidentiality, integrity, and availability are three brands of firewall
Confidentiality means only authorized staff see the records, integrity means the records are not altered, availability means the systems work when patients arrive
The triad only applies to hospitals, not small clinics
scenarios.why: Confidentiality protects information from unauthorized eyes, integrity protects it from unauthorized change, and availability keeps it usable when needed. The three words are a checklist: for any system, ask who should see it, whether it could be tampered with, and whether it will be there when needed.
scenarios.hint: Match each word to its plain meaning: secret, unaltered, reachable.

scenarios.title: Two proofs are better than one
scenarios.situation: A new employee logs in with a password, then taps approve on a prompt sent to their phone. A coworker says that is two-factor authentication; another says it is just logging in twice.
scenarios.prompt: Who is right, and why?
choices: The first coworker — the password is something you know and the phone is something you have: two different factor types
The second coworker — typing a password and tapping a phone are the same thing done twice
Neither — multi-factor requires three factors minimum
Both — the terms mean the same thing
scenarios.why: Authentication factors are categories: something you know (password), something you have (phone, token), something you are (fingerprint). Multi-factor means combining different categories, so stealing one is not enough. A password plus a password hint is still one factor.
scenarios.hint: Count the categories of proof, not the number of steps.

scenarios.title: The stolen password that went nowhere
scenarios.situation: An attacker buys a user's password from a breach dump and tries it on the company portal. The login fails because the portal also requires approving a push notification on the user's phone.
scenarios.prompt: Why did multi-factor authentication stop the attacker?
choices: The second factor is something the attacker does not have — a correct password alone is no longer enough
The password was too short for the attacker to type correctly
Breach dumps never contain real passwords
The portal was offline during the attack
scenarios.why: Passwords leak constantly through breaches, phishing, and reuse. MFA adds a second, independent proof — usually possession of a device — so a stolen password alone cannot complete the login. It is the single highest-value control most organizations can deploy.
scenarios.hint: What did the attacker have, and what were they missing?

scenarios.title: The lock anyone can close
scenarios.situation: A job applicant needs to send sensitive documents to a hiring manager securely. The manager publishes a public key and keeps a private key secret.
scenarios.prompt: How should the applicant protect the documents?
choices: Encrypt with the manager's private key, which the manager should share first
The public key decrypts, so send the documents in the clear and share the public key separately
Public and private keys are identical, so either one works for everything
Encrypt with the manager's public key — only the manager's private key can open them
scenarios.why: In asymmetric cryptography the keys are a matched pair with opposite jobs: the public key encrypts (anyone can lock), the private key decrypts (only the owner can open). The public key is shared freely; the private key is never shared. That is what makes secure communication with strangers possible.
scenarios.hint: Which key is safe to publish, and what job does each key do?

scenarios.title: The breached database with no passwords in it
scenarios.situation: A website is breached and its user database is stolen. The attackers find passwords stored as salted hashes, not plain text, and cannot log in as users.
scenarios.prompt: Why do systems store hashes instead of the actual passwords?
choices: Hashes are faster to type than passwords
Hashes make passwords impossible for users to forget
Hashing lets the system verify a password without storing the secret itself — a stolen database does not hand over the passwords
Storing plain text is illegal everywhere, so hashes are the only option
scenarios.why: A hash is a one-way fingerprint: the system hashes what you type and compares it to the stored hash, so the real password never sits in the database. When (not if) the database leaks, attackers get fingerprints they cannot reverse into passwords. Salting adds uniqueness so identical passwords hash differently.
scenarios.hint: What does the system actually compare when you log in?

scenarios.title: The window left open
scenarios.situation: A ground-floor office window does not lock. The neighborhood has seen several break-ins recently. The office manager asks whether this is actually a security risk worth fixing.
scenarios.prompt: What is the risk here, and what reduces it most directly?
choices: There is no risk — windows are not IT equipment
The risk is the window itself; remove all windows
Only the break-in statistics matter; the window is irrelevant
The risk is the chance that the threat (burglars) exploits the vulnerability (unlocked window); locking or securing the window reduces it
scenarios.why: Risk is the potential that a threat exploits a vulnerability to cause harm. The threat is the burglar, the vulnerability is the unlocked window, and the risk is the combination. You reduce risk by addressing either side — remove the vulnerability (lock the window) or reduce the threat — and the cheapest effective fix usually targets the vulnerability.
scenarios.hint: Name the threat, name the weakness, then see how they combine.

scenarios.title: The intern with the master key
scenarios.situation: To make onboarding easier, IT gives a new intern full administrator access to every system on day one. The intern only needs email and the shared drive.
scenarios.prompt: What principle does this violate, and what is the danger?
choices: Availability — the intern will slow the systems down
Encryption — the intern's laptop is not encrypted
Least privilege — grant only the access needed for the job; extra access magnifies both mistakes and breaches
No principle — more access is always better for productivity
scenarios.why: Least privilege means every person and process gets the minimum access needed — nothing more. An intern with admin rights can accidentally (or maliciously) cause damage far beyond their role, and if their account is compromised, the attacker inherits the keys to everything. Start small; add access only with justification.
scenarios.hint: What happens when this account — or its mistakes — gets more power than the job needs?

scenarios.title: The bakery that baked through ransomware
scenarios.situation: A bakery's order computer is hit by ransomware and every file is encrypted. The owner plugs in an external drive that is normally kept unplugged in a drawer, restores the files, and is taking orders again by lunch.
scenarios.prompt: What saved the bakery, and what made the backup trustworthy?
choices: Luck — ransomware usually decrypts itself after a few hours
Offline backups plus a restore plan — the drive was disconnected so the malware could not reach it, and the owner knew how to restore
The antivirus — it silently fixed everything
Paying the ransom quickly — the attackers sent the key
scenarios.why: Backups only save you if the disaster cannot reach them: an offline or disconnected copy survives ransomware that encrypts everything on the network. And a backup you have never restored is a rumor — the owner had practiced the restore, so recovery took hours instead of weeks.
scenarios.hint: Why didn't the ransomware encrypt the external drive too?

scenarios.title: Four hours or the wedding cakes do not ship
scenarios.situation: A bakery manager tells IT: if the order system is down more than four hours, the day's revenue is lost — and they can afford to lose at most one hour of entered orders.
scenarios.prompt: What are these two requirements called?
choices: RTO of four hours (how fast it must be back) and RPO of one hour (how much data loss is tolerable)
RPO of four hours and RTO of one hour — time and data are the same thing
An SLA and a password policy
Two ways of saying the system must never fail
scenarios.why: Recovery Time Objective (RTO) is how long the business can survive without the system; Recovery Point Objective (RPO) is how much data it can afford to lose, which sets how often backups must run. The business states them, IT builds recovery to meet them.
scenarios.hint: Which number is about the clock, and which is about the data?

scenarios.title: Do not pull the plug just yet
scenarios.situation: An employee sees a malware alert on their PC and is about to wipe the machine completely to get back to work. A coworker stops them and says to call IT first.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct first response, and why not wipe immediately?
choices: Wipe it — speed matters more than anything
Ignore the alert — antivirus handles everything silently
Disconnect from the network, leave the machine on, and report it — wiping destroys evidence of how the malware arrived and whether it spread
Email the malware to a friend to get a second opinion
scenarios.why: The first move in incident response is containment: disconnect the machine so the malware cannot spread, while preserving the system for investigation. Wiping first destroys the evidence that shows how the infection happened — and whether other machines are infected too. Report, contain, then let the response process decide.
scenarios.hint: If you wipe it, what questions can nobody ever answer?

scenarios.title: The plan for the people vs the plan for the computers
scenarios.situation: A burst pipe floods the office. Staff need somewhere to work on Monday, and the servers need to be brought back online. The manager pulls out two plans: the BCP and the DRP.
scenarios.prompt: What is the difference between the two plans?
choices: They are identical — the names are interchangeable
The BCP is for computers and the DRP is for people
Only large companies need either plan
The business continuity plan keeps the business running (alternate site, communications, key processes); the disaster recovery plan restores the IT systems
scenarios.why: Business continuity is about the business: where people work, how customers are served, which processes matter most. Disaster recovery is the IT subset: restoring servers, data, and networks. DRP feeds into BCP — technology recovery serves business survival, not the other way around.
scenarios.hint: Which plan cares about where the staff sit on Monday?

scenarios.title: The drill with no computers
scenarios.situation: The office team sits around a conference table and talks through what everyone would do if a flood hit the building. No systems are touched; it is all discussion.
scenarios.prompt: What is the value of this exercise?
choices: None — only real disasters teach anything
It tests the plan and everyone's role cheaply: gaps in contacts, responsibilities, and decisions surface before a real crisis
It replaces the need for backups
It is a team-building lunch with extra steps
scenarios.why: A tabletop exercise walks the team through a scenario verbally, revealing the gaps paper plans hide: outdated phone numbers, unclear decision authority, steps nobody owns. It costs an afternoon and finds the flaws while there is still time to fix them — which is the whole point of testing plans.
scenarios.hint: What is cheaper: finding the gap in a meeting, or during the flood?

scenarios.title: The laptop that might be evidence
scenarios.situation: A manager suspects a departing employee copied customer lists to a company laptop. IT is asked to examine it, and someone suggests just reimaging it quickly to reassign it.
scenarios.prompt: What must the team NOT do, and why?
choices: Do not wipe, reimage, or keep using the laptop — altering it destroys potential evidence of what was taken
Do not tell the manager — investigations should be secret from everyone
Do not document anything — paperwork slows investigations
There are no restrictions; reimage it immediately
scenarios.why: Once a device may hold evidence, every change to it — wiping, reinstalling, even browsing — can destroy proof of what happened and when. The correct move is to stop using it, secure it, document who handles it, and let the investigation process run. Evidence you alter is evidence you lose.
scenarios.hint: If this becomes a legal matter, what will lawyers ask about the laptop's history?

scenarios.title: The meeting after the mess
scenarios.situation: After a painful day-long outage, the team holds a meeting to discuss what went wrong and what to change. One person worries it will turn into a blame session.
scenarios.prompt: What is the purpose of this meeting, and how should it be run?
choices: To assign blame so people work harder next time
A blameless review to improve the plan and controls so the failure does not repeat — focus on process, not people
To decide who gets fired
There is no purpose; outages are unavoidable
scenarios.why: The lessons-learned (post-incident) review exists to convert a painful event into durable improvements: fix the plan, add the missing control, update the runbook. Blame makes people hide mistakes; a blameless focus on process gets honest answers — and honest answers are what prevent the repeat.
scenarios.hint: Do you want people to hide their mistakes, or report them?

scenarios.title: The new hire's first day
scenarios.situation: HR enters a new employee as an accountant in the identity system, and the correct email, file shares, and finance apps are provisioned automatically based on that role.
scenarios.prompt: What access control model is this?
choices: Discretionary access control — the employee decides their own access
Role-based access control — permissions are assigned to the role, and people inherit them by being in the role
Mandatory access control — the government assigned a clearance level
No model — this is just convenience
scenarios.why: Role-based access control (RBAC) ties permissions to job roles rather than individuals: join the accountant role, get accountant access; change roles, and access follows automatically. It scales far better than hand-crafting permissions per person, and it makes reviews simple — audit the role, not every user.
scenarios.hint: What did HR actually assign — permissions, or a job title that carries permissions?

scenarios.title: The folder owner shares
scenarios.situation: A team lead shares their project folder with a contractor for two weeks, choosing exactly which files the contractor can open.
scenarios.prompt: What model lets the data owner make that call?
choices: Mandatory access control — the system administrator must approve every share
Role-based access control — only the contractor role can be shared
No control — sharing is always insecure
Discretionary access control — the owner of the resource decides who gets access
scenarios.why: Discretionary access control (DAC) puts the owner in charge: the person who owns the file or folder decides who may access it. It is flexible and familiar — it is how most file sharing works — but it relies on owners making good decisions, which is why sensitive data usually needs stronger models.
scenarios.hint: Who made the sharing decision — a policy, or the person who owns the folder?

scenarios.title: The stamp that decides
scenarios.situation: Government documents carry labels like Confidential and Secret. The system compares each user's clearance to each document's label and grants or denies access automatically — no user can override it.
scenarios.prompt: What model is this?
choices: Mandatory access control — the system enforces access from security labels; users cannot change the rules
Discretionary — the document authors choose the readers
Role-based — everyone with the same job sees the same files
Voluntary — access is optional
scenarios.why: Mandatory access control (MAC) is system-enforced: labels on data (classification) and labels on users (clearance) decide access, and no user discretion can override them. It is strict and inflexible — which is exactly what environments with classified information require.
scenarios.hint: Can the document owner share it with a friend anyway? That is the test.

scenarios.title: The cashier who also approves refunds
scenarios.situation: One retail employee can both issue refunds and approve them. Last month, fake refunds totaling $9,000 went to an accomplice's account before anyone noticed.
scenarios.prompt: What control would have prevented a single person from doing this?
choices: Longer passwords for the cashier
More security cameras
A faster refund process
Separation of duties — split the task so issuing and approving require two different people; fraud then needs collusion
scenarios.why: Separation of duties divides sensitive tasks so no single person controls a process end to end. One person issuing and another approving means fraud requires two people conspiring — far rarer and far easier to detect. It is a people-and-process control, not a technology purchase.
scenarios.hint: How many people had to agree for the fraud to work? How many should it take?

scenarios.title: The friendly stranger with the coffee
scenarios.situation: An employee badges into the office and a stranger carrying two coffee cups follows them through the door, smiling and saying thanks. The stranger has no badge visible.
scenarios.prompt: What should the employee do?
choices: Politely stop them and direct them to reception to sign in and get a visitor badge — tailgating is a classic intrusion method
Hold the door — it is polite, and the coffee cups prove they work here
Ignore it — physical security is the guards' problem
Take a photo and post it online
scenarios.why: Tailgating (piggybacking) is one of the oldest intrusion techniques: follow an authorized person through a controlled door. The defense is cultural — every employee enforces the badge rule, politely but firmly, and visitors go through reception. Politeness is the attacker's tool; procedure is yours.
scenarios.hint: What is the attacker counting on you feeling?

scenarios.title: The account that outlived the employee
scenarios.situation: An employee left six months ago, but their account was never disabled. An attacker found the stale credentials in an old breach dump and used them to log in last week.
scenarios.prompt: What process failed, and what is the fix?
choices: Provisioning — accounts were created too slowly
Deprovisioning — accounts must be disabled promptly when people leave; tie it to the HR departure process
Encryption — the account was not encrypted
Backup — the account was not backed up
scenarios.why: Deprovisioning removes access when it is no longer needed — departures, role changes, contractors ending. Stale accounts are attacker favorites: nobody watches them, and their passwords never change. The fix is procedural: HR triggers IT on every departure, and access reviews catch what the process misses.
scenarios.hint: When should the account's life have ended?

scenarios.title: The curious coworker
scenarios.situation: An employee asks IT for a peek at a colleague's salary file, saying they are just curious and promise not to tell anyone.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct response?
choices: Share it — curiosity is harmless and they promised secrecy
Share it but ask them not to copy it
Post the salaries publicly so nobody has to ask
Deny the request — access requires a business need-to-know, not curiosity; even authorized staff only see what their job requires
scenarios.why: Need-to-know (a facet of least privilege) means access follows job necessity, not curiosity or seniority. Granting one-off peeks trains the organization that access rules are negotiable — and every exception is a precedent. The answer is a polite, firm no, with the request logged.
scenarios.hint: Does their job require this information?

scenarios.title: The bouncer at the door
scenarios.situation: A small office installs a firewall between their network and the internet. The owner asks what it actually does for them day to day.
scenarios.prompt: What is the firewall's job?
choices: It speeds up the internet connection
It encrypts every file on every computer
It blocks unsolicited inbound traffic and enforces rules about what may enter or leave — a bouncer with a guest list
It replaces the need for passwords
scenarios.why: A firewall is a policy enforcement point: it inspects traffic and allows or denies it based on rules — which addresses, ports, and directions are permitted. It does not encrypt your files or replace authentication; it controls the door so fewer attacks ever reach the inside.
scenarios.hint: Think about what a bouncer does — and does not do — at a club door.

scenarios.title: The customers on the company network
scenarios.situation: A cafe offers free Wi-Fi, but it runs on the same network as the point-of-sale system that processes card payments. A regular customer is studying networking.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with this setup, and what is the fix?
choices: The guest traffic shares a network with payment systems; isolate guest Wi-Fi on a separate network or VLAN away from business systems
Nothing — customers would never look at other devices
The Wi-Fi password should be removed to make it easier
The point-of-sale should be moved to the guest network
scenarios.why: Anyone on the same network can observe and potentially reach other devices on it. Guest traffic — untrusted by definition — must be segmented away from systems handling payments or business data. A separate guest network or VLAN is the standard, inexpensive fix.
scenarios.hint: Who else is on that network, and what could they reach?

scenarios.title: The laptop at the coffee shop
scenarios.situation: An employee needs to work from a coffee shop's public Wi-Fi and access files on the office server. Anyone nearby could be listening to the wireless traffic.
scenarios.prompt: How should the employee protect the connection?
choices: Turn the screen brightness down so nobody can read it
Only visit websites with nice designs
Public Wi-Fi is safe as long as you have antivirus
Use the company VPN — it encrypts traffic between the laptop and the office, shielding it from local eavesdroppers
scenarios.why: A virtual private network (VPN) builds an encrypted tunnel from the device to the trusted network, so anyone sniffing the coffee-shop Wi-Fi sees only scrambled traffic. It does not make the laptop itself secure — but it removes the network eavesdropper from the threat model.
scenarios.hint: What can the person at the next table see without protection?

scenarios.title: The router from 2012
scenarios.situation: An office access point still runs WEP security with the manufacturer's default admin password, and the network name broadcasts the company name.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct upgrade?
choices: Nothing — WEP was good enough in 2012 and nothing has changed
Move to WPA3 (or WPA2 at minimum), set a strong unique passphrase, and change the default admin credentials
Hide the network name — that alone stops attackers
Remove the password so guests connect easily
scenarios.why: WEP is broken — its encryption can be cracked in minutes — and default credentials are published in every manual online. Modern wireless security means WPA2 or WPA3 with a strong passphrase, unique admin credentials, and firmware updates. Hiding the network name (disabling SSID broadcast) is obscurity, not security.
scenarios.hint: Which of these settings would stop an attacker for more than a few minutes?

scenarios.title: The website that drowned
scenarios.situation: During the biggest sale of the year, an online store becomes unreachable. Traffic is a hundred times normal, coming from thousands of compromised devices worldwide — not real shoppers.
scenarios.prompt: What is happening, and what is the mitigation concept?
choices: A successful marketing campaign — buy a bigger server eventually
A worm — disconnect the store permanently
A distributed denial-of-service attack — absorb and filter the flood with a CDN, scrubbing service, or cloud scaling, and engage the ISP or provider
Normal holiday traffic — do nothing
scenarios.why: A DDoS attack overwhelms a target with traffic from a botnet, making the service unavailable to legitimate users — an attack on availability. You cannot block thousands of sources with a firewall rule; mitigation means absorbing the flood upstream (CDN, scrubbing centers, elastic scaling) and filtering attack traffic before it reaches you.
scenarios.hint: Is the goal to steal data, or to make the site unreachable?

scenarios.title: The free Wi-Fi that was not
scenarios.situation: At an airport, a traveler sees Free_Airport_WiFi with full signal and joins it. The hotspot is actually a laptop in an attacker's backpack, capturing every login the traveler types.
scenarios.prompt: How should travelers protect themselves from rogue hotspots?
choices: Always join the strongest free signal — signal strength proves legitimacy
Turn off the firewall to connect faster
Airports are safe, so no precautions are needed
Verify the official network name with staff, prefer a phone hotspot or VPN, and avoid sensitive logins on unknown networks
scenarios.why: An evil-twin attack mimics a legitimate hotspot to intercept traffic. Defenses: confirm the real network name with staff, use your phone's hotspot or a VPN so intercepted traffic is encrypted, and treat every unknown network as hostile. The attacker relies on convenience beating caution.
scenarios.hint: How would you know which hotspot is the real one?

scenarios.title: The open doors nobody uses
scenarios.situation: A scan of the office network finds an old printer with Telnet enabled — a service nobody uses or remembers configuring. The printer's firmware has not been updated in five years.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct action?
choices: Leave it — unused services cannot be attacked
Open more ports so the printer is easier to manage
Replace Telnet with a longer password
Disable the unneeded service and close the port — every open service is a potential entry point; shrink the attack surface
scenarios.why: Attack surface is the sum of reachable entry points: open ports, running services, enabled protocols. Unused services — especially ancient cleartext ones like Telnet — are pure risk with zero benefit. Hardening means disabling what you do not need, patching what you keep, and re-checking regularly.
scenarios.hint: What does the business gain from that open port? What could an attacker gain?

scenarios.title: The break-in with no witnesses
scenarios.situation: A server is compromised, but the company kept almost no logs. Nobody can say when the attacker got in, what they touched, or whether they are still inside.
scenarios.prompt: What is the lesson for security operations?
choices: Logs are optional — the antivirus will write the incident report
Centralized logging enables detection and investigation: without logs, you cannot see the attack or scope the damage
Delete logs regularly so attackers cannot read them
Only large companies need logging
scenarios.why: Logs are the witnesses of the digital world: they record who did what and when. Centralized collection (often in a SIEM) lets analysts detect patterns and reconstruct incidents. No logs means no timeline, no scope, and no confident recovery — you are guessing in the dark.
scenarios.hint: What would a detective say about a crime scene with no witnesses and no cameras?

scenarios.title: The update everyone postponed
scenarios.situation: Attackers breach a company through a vulnerability the vendor patched eight months ago. The patch was marked low priority and never scheduled.
scenarios.prompt: What process failed, and what does good look like?
choices: Patch management — inventory systems, test patches, and deploy them on a schedule; known vulnerabilities are the attacker's favorite door
Antivirus — it should have stopped a patched vulnerability
Hiring — the team needed more people to ignore updates
Nothing failed — patching is optional
scenarios.why: Most breaches exploit known vulnerabilities with available patches — attackers automate scanning for unpatched systems within hours of disclosure. Patch management is the disciplined cycle: know what you have, test the fix, deploy it promptly, and verify. Postponed patches are open invitations.
scenarios.hint: Did the attackers discover something new, or use something everyone knew about?

scenarios.title: The admin admin camera
scenarios.situation: An attacker logs into the office security cameras using the default username and password printed in the manufacturer's manual, then watches the building for weeks.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix, and what broader practice does it belong to?
choices: Change all default credentials as part of system hardening — defaults are public knowledge, not secrets
Unplug the cameras — they are the problem
The manual should be kept secret instead
Longer camera cables
scenarios.why: Default credentials are published in manuals and online lists — attackers try them first. Hardening a system means changing defaults, disabling unneeded services, and applying secure baselines before it touches the network. Every device with admin/admin still set is an open door with a welcome mat.
scenarios.hint: Where else could an attacker find that default password?

scenarios.title: The email that looked like the boss
scenarios.situation: An employee receives an urgent email that appears to be from the CEO, asking them to buy gift cards for client gifts and send the codes immediately.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct action?
choices: Do not reply or buy anything; report it to IT or security through the phishing report button — this is a classic gift-card scam
Buy the gift cards — the CEO's name is on the email
Reply asking which store the CEO prefers
Forward it to friends so they can get gift cards too
scenarios.why: No executive requests gift cards by email — urgency plus an unusual request is the signature of this scam. The right move is to stop, not engage, and report it so security can warn others and block the sender. Reporting turns one near-miss into protection for the whole company.
scenarios.hint: Has your CEO ever asked anyone to buy gift cards by email?

scenarios.title: The spreadsheet marked confidential
scenarios.situation: The company labels data as Public, Internal, or Confidential. A new employee wonders why a customer list marked Confidential cannot be emailed to a personal account for weekend work.
scenarios.prompt: Why does classification matter?
choices: Labels are decoration — data is data
Only the CEO may see Confidential data
Public data needs the strongest protection
Classification drives handling rules: Confidential data gets encryption, sharing limits, and retention rules matched to its sensitivity
scenarios.why: Data classification assigns each type of information a sensitivity level, and each level carries handling rules: how it is stored, shared, encrypted, and eventually destroyed. Without labels, everything is treated the same — which means the crown jewels get the same protection as the lunch menu.
scenarios.hint: Should the lunch menu and the customer database be protected identically?

scenarios.title: The laptop left on the train
scenarios.situation: An employee leaves a laptop on a train. It holds customer records — but the entire disk was encrypted, and the loss is reported within the hour so the password can be rotated and the device remotely locked.
scenarios.prompt: Why is this incident a recovery story instead of a data breach?
choices: The train company is trustworthy
Full-disk encryption keeps the data unreadable without the key — a lost encrypted device is a hardware loss, not a data exposure
Customer records are not sensitive
Encryption only matters for email
scenarios.why: Encryption at rest protects data on lost or stolen devices: without the key, the disk is scrambled noise to whoever finds it. Paired with quick reporting, remote lock, and credential rotation, the incident stays a lost laptop instead of becoming a breach notification. Encrypt mobile devices by default — loss is a matter of when.
scenarios.hint: What can the finder actually read on that disk?

scenarios.title: The one screen that watches everything
scenarios.situation: A small security team is drowning in separate logs from firewalls, servers, and laptops. They deploy a SIEM that pulls the logs into one place and raises alerts on suspicious patterns.
scenarios.prompt: What value does the SIEM add for a junior analyst?
choices: Centralized collection plus correlation and alerting: one place to search, and patterns across sources surface automatically instead of checking devices one by one
It replaces analysts entirely — the SIEM makes all decisions
It makes the logs prettier
It deletes old logs to save disk space
scenarios.why: A SIEM (security information and event management) centralizes logs so analysts can search everything at once, and its correlation rules connect events across sources into meaningful alerts. It does not replace judgment — it focuses it: fewer places to look, higher-quality leads to investigate.
scenarios.hint: What is harder: checking fifty devices, or searching one screen?

lessons.title: Security Principles — Core concepts
concepts: CIA triad: confidentiality (only the right eyes see it), integrity (it is not altered), availability (it is there when needed). Three words that organize nearly every security question you will ever face.
Authentication factors: something you know (password), something you have (phone, token), something you are (fingerprint). Multi-factor combines different types, so one stolen secret is not enough.

Cryptography basics: symmetric uses one shared key (fast, but sharing the key is the hard part); asymmetric uses a public key to lock and a private key to open; hashing fingerprints data one-way for integrity.
Risk = threat x vulnerability x impact, in plain language: a bad actor, a weakness they can use, and harm if they succeed. Reduce any of the three and risk falls.
Least privilege: give every person and process the minimum access the job needs — nothing more. It limits both accidents and attackers.

example.code:
Password alone: attacker with a breach dump logs straight in.
Password + phone approval: the same stolen password goes nowhere.
example.walkthrough: The second factor did not make the password stronger — it made the password insufficient on its own. That is the whole idea of defense in depth: no single failure hands over the keys.

pitfalls: Common trap: thinking a username plus a password is two factors — it is one factor used twice.
Common trap: confusing encryption with hashing — encryption is reversible with the key; hashing is one-way.
Common trap: believing more access is helpful — extra permissions multiply the damage of every mistake and breach.
Common trap: treating risk as only a technical problem — people and process are usually the weakest link.
lessons.try_it: Verify a file's hash yourself in the Terminal tab →

lessons.title: Business Continuity & Incident Response — Core concepts
concepts: Business continuity (BCP) keeps the business running through disruption: alternate sites, communications, and the processes that matter most. Disaster recovery (DRP) is the IT subset — restoring servers, data, and networks.
Backups must survive the disaster: keep copies offline or off-site so ransomware and fires cannot reach them, and practice restores — an untested backup is a rumor.
RTO is how fast a system must be back; RPO is how much data loss is tolerable. The business states them; IT builds recovery to meet them.
Incident response order: detect, contain, investigate, eradicate, recover, learn. Containment before cleanup — wiping first destroys evidence and lets the threat spread.
Tabletop exercises test the plan around a table for the cost of an afternoon; lessons-learned reviews convert each incident into a better plan. Blame-free, or people hide the truth.

example.code:
Ransomware encrypts the file server AND the network backup.
The offline drive in the drawer: untouched. Recovery by lunch.
example.walkthrough: The disaster reached everything it could touch. Continuity planning is about deciding in advance what it cannot touch — and proving the restore works before you need it.

pitfalls: Common trap: backing up to the same network the ransomware can reach — that is a copy, not a backup.
Common trap: wiping an infected machine before containing and investigating — speed that destroys evidence.
Common trap: writing a plan and never testing it — paper plans fail at the first outdated phone number.
Common trap: skipping the lessons-learned review — the incident repeats, with interest.
lessons.try_it: Confirm a backup exists in the Terminal tab →

lessons.title: Access Control Concepts — Core concepts
concepts: Three classic models: DAC — the data owner decides who gets access; MAC — the system enforces access from security labels, no overrides; RBAC — permissions attach to roles, people inherit them by role.
Least privilege and need-to-know: access follows job necessity, not curiosity, seniority, or convenience. Start small; add only with justification.
Separation of duties: split sensitive tasks so no one person controls a process end to end — fraud then requires collusion, which is rarer and easier to catch.
Account lifecycle: provision promptly on arrival, adjust on role change, and deprovision immediately on departure. Stale accounts are attacker favorites.
Physical controls matter: badges, locks, visitor sign-in, and a culture where everyone challenges tailgaters. The best firewall cannot stop a held door.

example.code:
One employee issues refunds AND approves them → $9,000 in fake refunds.
Split the duties → the same fraud now needs two conspirators.
example.walkthrough: No technology was purchased. Moving one approval to a second person changed the fraud from a solo act into a conspiracy — that is the power of a process control.

pitfalls: Common trap: giving new hires full access to make onboarding easy — convenience now, breach later.
Common trap: holding the door for a stranger with coffee — politeness is the tailgater's tool.
Common trap: forgetting to disable accounts when people leave — audit the leavers, not just the joiners.
Common trap: confusing identification (who you claim to be) with authentication (proving it).
lessons.try_it: Audit a shared folder's permissions in the Terminal tab →

lessons.title: Network Security — Core concepts
concepts: A firewall enforces rules about what traffic may enter or leave — a bouncer with a guest list. It controls the door; it does not encrypt files or replace passwords.
Segmentation separates trust levels: guest Wi-Fi away from payment systems, servers away from workstations. A breach in one zone should not mean a breach in all zones.
A VPN encrypts traffic between a device and a trusted network, defeating local eavesdroppers on public Wi-Fi. It protects the path, not the endpoints.
Wireless basics: WPA2/WPA3 with a strong passphrase, unique admin credentials, updated firmware. WEP is broken; hidden network names are obscurity, not security.
DDoS attacks overwhelm availability with floods from botnets — mitigate upstream with CDNs, scrubbing, and scaling, not with a bigger firewall rule.
Attack surface is the sum of reachable entry points. Disable unneeded services, close unneeded ports, and re-check: every open door is a door you must defend.

example.code:
Cafe Wi-Fi + point-of-sale on one network → any customer can reach the card terminal.
Guest network segmented away → the terminal is invisible to guests.
example.walkthrough: Segmentation does not make either network more secure in isolation — it stops a problem in one from becoming a problem in the other. Boundaries are the architecture.

pitfalls: Common trap: assuming the firewall makes everything behind it safe — one phished laptop is already inside.
Common trap: leaving WEP or default passwords on wireless gear — both are public knowledge to attackers.
Common trap: treating a bigger pipe as DDoS protection — floods scale faster than your bandwidth.
Common trap: leaving forgotten services running — the Telnet on that old printer is an unlocked window.
lessons.try_it: List listening services in the Terminal tab →

lessons.title: Security Operations — Core concepts
concepts: Logging is the foundation: without logs you cannot detect, investigate, or scope incidents. Centralize them (often in a SIEM) so one search covers everything.
Patch management is a cycle: inventory what you have, test the fix, deploy promptly, verify. Known vulnerabilities with available patches cause most breaches.
Hardening means secure by default: change default credentials, disable unneeded services, apply baselines before systems touch the network.
Awareness turns people into sensors: teach the signs of phishing, make reporting one click, and celebrate reports. Punishment drives incidents underground.
Data classification (Public, Internal, Confidential) drives handling rules: encryption, sharing limits, retention, and destruction matched to sensitivity.
Encryption at rest protects data on lost devices; encryption in transit protects it on hostile networks. Know which one each situation needs.

example.code:
No logs → 'we think we're clean, but we can't prove it.'
Centralized logs → 'the attacker entered Tuesday at 2 AM via this account.'
example.walkthrough: The difference between guessing and knowing is the log trail. Operations is mostly this: collect the evidence routinely, so the investigation is possible when it counts.

pitfalls: Common trap: treating the SIEM as a replacement for analysts — it focuses judgment; it does not replace it.
Common trap: postponing patches because nothing has happened yet — quiet is not the same as safe.
Common trap: assuming awareness training is a one-time video — behavior change needs repetition and measurement.
Common trap: encrypting everything identically — match protection to classification, or nothing gets the protection it needs.
lessons.try_it: Spot failed logins in the Terminal tab →

lessons.title: Security Principles: CIA, Risk, Controls, and Governance
concepts: The CIA triad is the foundation of all security thinking. Confidentiality ensures only authorized parties can access data — achieved through encryption, access controls, and classification. Integrity ensures data is accurate and is changed only by authorized actions — achieved through hashing, checksums, digital signatures, and change control. Availability ensures data and systems are reachable when needed — achieved through redundancy, backups, patching, and denial-of-service defenses. Nearly every exam question about 'which principle' maps to one of these three.

Risk is the combination of a threat (anything that could cause harm, such as ransomware) and a vulnerability (a weakness the threat can exploit, such as unpatched software). Formally, risk exists where a threat meets a vulnerability and an asset is exposed. Qualitative risk analysis ranks risks with labels like high/medium/low; quantitative analysis uses numbers: single loss expectancy (SLE) is the cost of one incident, annualized rate of occurrence (ARO) is how often it is expected per year, and annualized loss expectancy (ALE) equals SLE times ARO. Controls are judged by comparing their cost against the ALE reduction they deliver.

Security controls are described two ways. By function: preventive controls stop incidents (firewalls, mantraps, least privilege), detective controls spot them (IDS, CCTV, log monitoring), corrective controls restore normal operations (backups, incident response), deterrent controls discourage attackers (warning banners, visible guards), and compensating controls substitute when the ideal control is impractical. By category: administrative controls are policies and procedures, technical (logical) controls are hardware and software mechanisms, and physical controls are tangible barriers and devices. Defense in depth layers controls across both dimensions so no single failure is fatal.

Governance turns security intent into organizational reality. Policies are high-level statements of management intent; standards mandate specific technologies or configurations; procedures are step-by-step instructions; guidelines are recommended (not mandatory) best practices; baselines define minimum security configurations. Data classification (for example public, internal, confidential, restricted) drives handling rules, with data owners deciding classification, custodians implementing protections, and users following the rules.

Professional ethics matter at the entry level too. The ISC2 Code of Ethics binds members to four canons: protect society, the commonwealth, and the infrastructure; act honorably, honestly, justly, responsibly, and legally; provide diligent and competent service to principals; and advance and protect the profession. When a scenario pits convenience against integrity, the ethical answer follows these canons.

example.code:
# Quantitative risk: is a $12,000/year control worth it?
SLE=40000        # cost of one breach
ARO_BEFORE=0.5   # once every two years
ARO_AFTER=0.1    # with the control
COST=12000

ALE_BEFORE=$(echo "$SLE * $ARO_BEFORE" | bc)
ALE_AFTER=$(echo "$SLE * $ARO_AFTER" | bc)
SAVINGS=$(echo "$ALE_BEFORE - $ALE_AFTER" | bc)

echo "ALE before: \$$ALE_BEFORE /yr"
echo "ALE after:  \$$ALE_AFTER /yr"
echo "Savings:    \$$SAVINGS /yr vs cost \$$COST /yr"
if [ "$SAVINGS" -gt "$COST" ]; then
  echo "Decision: IMPLEMENT (savings exceed cost)"
else
  echo "Decision: REJECT (cost exceeds savings)"
fi
example.walkthrough: This script implements the ALE = SLE x ARO formula from the lesson. It computes the annualized loss expectancy before the control ($20,000) and after ($4,000), derives the $16,000 yearly savings, and compares it to the $12,000 control cost. Because savings exceed cost, the control is cost-justified — the same arithmetic behind scenario isc2-cc-sc2. Notice the script never claims risk reaches zero: a residual ALE of $4,000 remains for management to accept, transfer, or reduce further.

pitfalls: Encryption protects confidentiality, not integrity — an encrypted file can still be corrupted; integrity needs hashing or signatures.
Risk can be reduced, transferred (insurance), accepted, or avoided — but never eliminated entirely.
Deterrent is not the same as preventive: a warning banner discourages but does not block, while a firewall blocks.
Policies state intent; procedures give steps. Mixing them up is a classic exam trap.
lessons.try_it: Walk through your home setup and name one preventive, one detective, and one corrective control you already have (for example: a door lock, a smoke detector, and a backup drive). Then classify each as administrative, technical, or physical.

lessons.title: Continuity, Recovery, and Incident Response
concepts: Business continuity planning (BCP) keeps the business operating during a disruption; disaster recovery planning (DRP) restores IT systems afterward. The business impact analysis (BIA) is the foundation of both: it identifies critical processes, their dependencies, and how much pain an outage causes. From the BIA come the recovery targets: the recovery time objective (RTO) is the maximum tolerable downtime, the recovery point objective (RPO) is the maximum tolerable data loss measured in time, and the maximum tolerable downtime (MTD) is the absolute limit before the business faces existential harm. RTO must never exceed MTD, and RPO drives backup frequency.

Backups are the core corrective control. A full backup copies everything; an incremental backup copies changes since the last backup of any kind (fast to take, slow to restore — you need the full plus every incremental); a differential backup copies changes since the last full (slower to take than incremental, faster to restore — you need only the full plus the latest differential). The widely cited 3-2-1 rule keeps three copies of data on two different media with one copy offsite. Backups must be tested — an untested backup is a hope, not a control — and at least one copy should be offline or immutable so ransomware cannot encrypt it.

Recovery sites come in three flavors. A hot site is fully equipped and can take over in hours but costs the most. A warm site has hardware and connectivity but needs configuration, taking days. A cold site is just space and power, taking weeks but costing the least. The choice follows the RTO: the shorter the RTO, the hotter (and pricier) the site. Reciprocal agreements, where two organizations host each other's recovery capability, are a budget alternative.

Incident response follows NIST Special Publication 800-61's four-phase lifecycle. Preparation builds the team, tools, playbooks, and communication plans before anything happens. Detection and Analysis identifies and triages potential incidents using alerts, logs, and user reports. Containment, Eradication, and Recovery limits the blast radius, removes the cause, and restores systems to normal. Post-Incident Activity captures lessons learned and feeds improvements back into preparation. Skipping straight to recovery without containment and eradication is how incidents recur.

Communication discipline matters during incidents: know who declares an incident, who talks to executives, legal, and regulators, and what gets documented for the post-incident review. Evidence handling — preserving logs and forensic images with a documented chain of custody — keeps response options (including legal ones) open.

example.code:
INCIDENT: Ransomware notes on 3 workstations, 08:04 Monday

Phase 1 - Preparation (already done before the incident):
  IR team roster, playbook, and call tree existed; backups
  were tested last month; an offline backup copy is available.

Phase 2 - Detection and Analysis:
  08:04  Help desk tickets + ransom notes = confirmed incident
  08:15  Analyst scopes: 3 hosts, same subnet, same file share

Phase 3 - Containment, Eradication, and Recovery:
  08:20  CONTAIN: disconnect the 3 hosts from the network
  09:00  ERADICATE: reimage hosts from known-good media
  10:30  RECOVER: restore file share from offline backup,
           verify hashes, return to service

Phase 4 - Post-Incident Activity:
  Root cause: unpatched SMB service. Actions: emergency
  patching, network segmentation for the subnet, phishing
  refresher, playbook update. Lessons-learned report filed.
example.walkthrough: This walkthrough applies the NIST 800-61 lifecycle to the ransomware scenario from isc2-cc-sc4. Note the ordering discipline: containment (isolate) comes before eradication (reimage), which comes before recovery (restore) — restoring before eradicating would just re-infect the systems. Preparation done earlier (tested, offline backups) is what makes the recovery phase possible at all. The post-incident phase converts the pain into durable improvements, closing the loop back to preparation.

pitfalls: Restoring from backup before eradicating the malware re-infects the systems — containment and eradication come first.
Confusing RTO (how fast to recover) with RPO (how much data you can lose) — RPO drives backup frequency, RTO drives recovery-site choice.
Incremental restores need the full plus EVERY incremental in sequence; forgetting one breaks the chain.
An untested backup is not a control. Test restores on a schedule and document the results.
lessons.try_it: Write a one-page incident playbook for 'laptop stolen from a car': list your detection step, your containment step, your eradication/recovery steps, and two lessons-learned actions. Time yourself — playbooks are written before the incident, not during it.

lessons.title: Access Control: IAAA, MFA, Protocols, and Models
concepts: Access control runs on IAAA: Identification (claiming an identity, e.g., typing a username), Authentication (proving it, e.g., entering a password), Authorization (what the proven identity is allowed to do), and Accountability (logging actions so they can be traced to the identity). Authentication must precede authorization — the system cannot decide what you may do until it knows who you are — and accountability depends on the logs capturing all of it.

Authentication factors come in three categories: something you know (passwords, PINs), something you have (phones, hardware tokens, smart cards), and something you are (fingerprints, face, voice). Multi-factor authentication (MFA) requires two or more factors from different categories; two steps within the same category (password plus security question) is still single-factor. Biometrics are convenient but irrevocable — you cannot reissue a fingerprint — so they are best paired with another factor and protected accordingly.

Common authentication protocols each have a home turf. Kerberos is the ticket-based LAN standard (used by Active Directory). LDAP (often LDAPS) provides directory lookups for identity data. RADIUS and TACACS+ centralize AAA for network devices, with TACACS+ separating authentication, authorization, and accounting and encrypting the full payload. SAML 2.0 is the XML standard for federated web single sign-on via identity-provider assertions. OAuth 2.0 is an authorization/delegation framework — often paired with OpenID Connect for authentication — dominant in APIs and mobile apps. CHAP and PAP are legacy PPP authentication protocols; EAP frameworks underpin WPA-Enterprise wireless authentication.

Authorization models decide who gets what. DAC (discretionary) lets data owners grant access at their discretion, as with file ACLs. MAC (mandatory) has the system enforce access from security labels and clearances that users cannot override — the government and military model. RBAC (role-based) assigns permissions to job roles and users to roles, simplifying administration and supporting least privilege. ABAC (attribute-based) evaluates attributes of the subject, resource, action, and environment for fine-grained, context-aware decisions. Rule-based access control applies global rules (such as time-of-day restrictions) uniformly.

Account management and physical controls complete the picture. Provisioning grants access on hire or role change, deprovisioning revokes it promptly on departure — orphaned accounts are a classic attack path. Least privilege gives users only the access their role requires, enforced through periodic access reviews and separation of duties for sensitive processes. Physical controls — mantraps, badge readers, biometrics, CCTV, bollards, cable locks, visitor logs — protect the facilities where the technical controls live.

example.code:
DECISION: partner engineers need web-portal access

Requirement: sign in once with the corporate identity
provider, then use the partner's browser-based CAD portal
with no second login. The partner must trust our
authentication.

Candidate protocols:
  Kerberos .... LAN ticket system; does not cross the
                public internet to another organization.
  RADIUS ...... AAA for network devices, not browser SSO.
  OAuth 2.0 ... delegation for APIs/mobile apps; the
                classic enterprise web-SSO standard is older.
  SAML 2.0 .... XML assertions from an identity provider
                to a service provider; built for federated
                browser SSO.

Choice: SAML 2.0. The corporate IdP issues signed
assertions; the partner's portal (service provider)
validates them and creates the session. No partner-side
passwords to manage, and deprovisioning at the IdP
instantly cuts partner access too.
example.walkthrough: This is the reasoning behind scenario isc2-cc-sc9. The key discriminator is 'browser-based SSO across organizational boundaries' — that phrase points to federation, and the enterprise federation standard is SAML 2.0. OAuth 2.0 plus OpenID Connect is the modern alternative many SaaS apps use, but SAML remains the canonical answer for cross-company web SSO. Note the operational bonus: centralizing authentication at the identity provider means one deprovisioning action revokes access everywhere.

pitfalls: Two steps are not automatically MFA — a password plus a security question is still one factor (something you know).
Authentication proves who you are; authorization decides what you may do. SSO authenticates once — it does not grant universal authorization.
SSO is convenient but a single point of failure: protect the identity provider with MFA and monitor it closely.
Biometrics identify but cannot be revoked — never use them as the sole factor for high-value access.
lessons.try_it: List every account you own that protects money or identity. Mark which have MFA enabled and which factor types they use. Enable MFA (preferably an authenticator app or hardware key over SMS) on any that lack it.

lessons.title: Network Security: Layers, Segmentation, and Wireless
concepts: The OSI model gives every attack an address. Layer 1 (Physical): wiretaps, signal jamming. Layer 2 (Data Link): MAC flooding, ARP spoofing/poisoning. Layer 3 (Network): IP spoofing, ICMP attacks, rogue routing. Layer 4 (Transport): SYN floods, port scanning, session hijacking at the TCP level. Layer 5 (Session): session hijacking and fixation. Layer 6 (Presentation): SSL/TLS stripping and encryption abuse. Layer 7 (Application): phishing, SQL injection, cross-site scripting (XSS), DNS poisoning, and malware delivery. Mapping an attack to its layer immediately suggests the right control.

Segmentation limits blast radius. VLANs separate broadcast domains at Layer 2; subnetting separates them at Layer 3; a DMZ (demilitarized zone) is a screened subnet for public-facing services between the internet and the internal network; microsegmentation applies fine-grained policy around individual workloads. The design rule is simple: internet-facing services live in the DMZ, sensitive data lives inside, and firewalls enforce least-privilege traffic between zones.

Firewalls and intrusion systems are complementary, not interchangeable. Packet-filtering firewalls judge individual packets by header fields; stateful firewalls track connection state; next-generation firewalls (NGFW) add application awareness, user identity, and threat intelligence. An IDS (intrusion detection system) watches and alerts — passive, usually placed to monitor traffic via a span port or tap. An IPS (intrusion prevention system) sits inline and can block — active, but a misconfigured IPS can break legitimate traffic. Honeypots and honeynets are decoy systems that attract attackers and generate high-fidelity alerts.

VPNs extend private networks across untrusted ones. Site-to-site VPNs connect whole networks (branch to headquarters), typically with IPsec. Remote-access VPNs connect individual users, commonly with IPsec or TLS/SSL VPNs. IPsec operates at the network layer and offers tunnel mode (gateway to gateway) and transport mode (host to host), with AH providing integrity and ESP providing confidentiality plus integrity. TLS VPNs work through the browser or a lightweight client and traverse NAT and restrictive firewalls more easily.

Wireless security has evolved hard lessons. WEP is broken and must never be used; WPA2 (AES-CCMP) was the long standard; WPA3 is current, adding stronger handshakes (SAE) and forward secrecy, with WPA3-Enterprise using 802.1X and certificates for mutual authentication. Threats include rogue access points, evil twins (impersonating the legitimate SSID to harvest credentials), deauthentication attacks, and wardriving. Mitigations: WPA3-Enterprise with 802.1X, a wireless intrusion prevention system (WIPS) to find rogues, and disabling auto-connect on managed devices.

example.code:
# Reviewing a firewall ruleset for dangerous permits
$ cat fw-rules.txt
-A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -s 10.0.0.0/8 -j ACCEPT
-A INPUT -p tcp --dport 80 -j ACCEPT
-A INPUT -p tcp --dport 443 -j ACCEPT
-A INPUT -p tcp --dport 23 -j ACCEPT
-A INPUT -p tcp --dport 3389 -s 0.0.0.0/0 -j ACCEPT
-A INPUT -j DROP

# Which services are exposed, and to whom?
$ grep ACCEPT fw-rules.txt | awk '{print $4, $6, $8}'
--dport 22 -s 10.0.0.0/8     # SSH: internal only. OK.
--dport 80                  # HTTP: open to the world. Expected for a web server.
--dport 443                 # HTTPS: open to the world. Expected.
--dport 23                  # TELNET: open to the world. FINDING!
--dport 3389 -s 0.0.0.0/0   # RDP: open to the world. FINDING!

# Findings: Telnet (23) sends credentials in cleartext and
# should be disabled; RDP (3389) exposed to 0.0.0.0/0 invites
# brute force. Remediation: remove the Telnet rule, restrict
# RDP to the management subnet or require VPN + MFA.
example.walkthrough: This example shows the core network-security review skill: read the ruleset, map each permitted port to a service and a source, and flag violations of least privilege. Telnet is the louder finding because it transmits credentials in cleartext (a confidentiality failure at Layer 7 riding on Layer 4). RDP open to the world is the classic brute-force target seen in scenario isc2-cc-sc15's SIEM pattern. The final default-DROP rule is the correct posture: deny everything not explicitly permitted.

pitfalls: An IDS detects and alerts; only an IPS can block. Placing an IDS inline expecting prevention is a design error.
NAT hides internal addresses but is not a security boundary — it was designed for address conservation.
Hiding the SSID or filtering MAC addresses is obscurity, not security; both are trivially bypassed.
WEP is cryptographically broken. Any question offering WEP as acceptable is a trap.
lessons.try_it: On your home router's admin page, check three things: is remote administration disabled on the WAN interface, is WPS turned off, and is the Wi-Fi using WPA2 or WPA3 (not WEP, not open)? Change anything that fails.

lessons.title: Security Operations: Logging, Crypto, Malware, and Hardening
concepts: Logging and monitoring turn noise into signal. Log authentication events, privilege use, system changes, and network connections; synchronize all clocks with NTP so timestamps correlate across systems; protect logs from tampering by forwarding them to a central, append-only store with restricted access; and retain them per policy and legal requirements. A SIEM (security and information event management) aggregates logs, normalizes them, correlates events into timelines, and raises alerts on defined rules — the '4,000 failures then one success' pattern from scenario isc2-cc-sc15 is exactly what correlation rules catch. SOAR platforms extend this by orchestrating automated response playbooks.

Cryptography provides confidentiality, integrity, authentication, and non-repudiation. Symmetric encryption (one shared key, e.g., AES-256) is fast and suits bulk data. Asymmetric encryption (public/private key pairs, e.g., RSA, elliptic-curve ECC) solves key distribution and enables signatures but is slower. Hashing (e.g., SHA-256) is one-way: it produces a fixed-size digest for integrity checking but cannot be reversed — hashing is not encryption. HMAC combines a hash with a secret key for authenticated integrity. Digital signatures (hash encrypted with the sender's private key) prove authenticity, integrity, and non-repudiation. PKI (public key infrastructure) with certificate authorities (CAs) binds public keys to identities, underpinning TLS. Key management — generation, distribution, rotation, and destruction — is where real-world crypto usually fails.

Malware comes in recognizable families. A virus needs a host file and user action; a worm self-replicates across networks without user action; a trojan masquerades as legitimate software; ransomware encrypts data and demands payment; spyware and keyloggers steal information silently; a rootkit buries itself to maintain privileged hidden access; a RAT (remote access trojan) gives attackers interactive control; logic bombs trigger on a condition. Defenses layer antivirus/EDR, patching, application allow-listing, email filtering, backups, and user awareness.

Hardening reduces attack surface before attacks arrive. Apply patches promptly, disable unnecessary services and ports, remove default credentials, enforce least privilege, configure baselines and audit against them, enable host firewalls with default-deny, encrypt data at rest and in transit, and deploy endpoint protection. Every open port and running service is a promise to defend — make fewer promises.

Social engineering bypasses technology by targeting people. Phishing is bulk fraudulent email; spear phishing targets specific individuals with researched lures; whaling targets executives; vishing uses voice calls; pretexting invents a scenario to extract information; baiting dangles something tempting (like an infected USB drive). Defenses: verify through independent channels, hover before clicking, report suspicious messages, and train continuously — the human is both the target and a sensor.

example.code:
# Integrity checking with SHA-256 hashes
$ printf 'Contract v3 - payment $50,000\n' > contract.txt
$ openssl dgst -sha256 contract.txt
SHA2-256(contract.txt)= 8f3a...c41d

# The recipient recomputes the hash on arrival:
$ openssl dgst -sha256 contract.txt
SHA2-256(contract.txt)= 8f3a...c41d   # match -> unaltered

# Now simulate tampering in transit:
$ printf 'Contract v3 - payment $90,000\n' > contract.txt
$ openssl dgst -sha256 contract.txt
SHA2-256(contract.txt)= 1b77...e902   # DIFFERENT -> tampered!

# A hash detects change but not the author. For proof of
# origin, the sender signs the hash with their private key:
$ openssl dgst -sha256 -sign legal.key -out contract.sig contract.txt
$ openssl dgst -sha256 -verify legal.pub -signature contract.sig contract.txt
Verified OK
example.walkthrough: This demonstrates the two halves of scenario isc2-cc-sc14. Hashing alone gives integrity: any alteration, even one character, produces a completely different digest (the avalanche effect), so the recipient detects tampering by recomputing. But a hash cannot prove who created the file — an attacker could alter the file and recompute the hash. The digital signature fixes that: only Legal's private key could have produced a signature that verifies with Legal's public key, delivering authenticity and non-repudiation on top of integrity.

pitfalls: Hashing is not encryption — a hash cannot be 'decrypted' back into the data, and it provides no confidentiality.
Encrypting with your own private key does not give confidentiality — anyone with your public key can read it; that operation is a signature.
Logs without synchronized time (NTP) cannot be correlated — timestamps become fiction across systems.
Security through obscurity (hidden SSIDs, secret algorithms) is not a control; Kerckhoffs's principle says the system must stay secure even when the design is public.
lessons.try_it: Pick any file on your computer and run `openssl dgst -sha256` (or `certutil -hashfile` on Windows / `shasum -a 256` on macOS) on it twice. Confirm the digests match, then change one byte and watch the digest change completely.

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you learned a difficult technical concept quickly. How did you approach it?
points: The concept and why it was hard for you
Your specific learning method — labs, docs, teaching it back
How you proved you actually understood it
pitfalls: Saying you just watched videos with no practice
No evidence you retained it

behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you noticed something suspicious — at work, school, or online — and what you did about it.
points: What caught your attention and why it felt off
The exact steps you took — verify, report, contain
The outcome and what you would do the same or differently
pitfalls: Ignoring it and hoping someone else handled it
Overreacting without verifying first

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you had to follow strict rules or procedures even when it was inconvenient.
points: The rule and why it felt inconvenient in the moment
Why you followed it anyway
What the experience taught you about process
pitfalls: Admitting you bent the rule
Resenting the process with no understanding of its purpose

behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you explained something technical to someone non-technical.
points: The concept and who your audience was
How you adapted — analogies, plain language, checking understanding
Whether they actually got it, and how you knew
pitfalls: Using jargon and calling it an explanation
No check that the audience understood

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you made a mistake involving important information or access. What happened and what changed?
points: The mistake, owned honestly and briefly
How you contained it and who you told
The lasting change — checklist, habit, or process
pitfalls: Hiding the mistake or minimizing it
No change afterward — same risk remains

behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you worked with a team under a tight deadline.
points: The deadline and what was at stake
Your specific role and how you coordinated with others
The result and what the pressure taught you
pitfalls: Taking all the credit or blaming the team
No reflection on teamwork itself

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you helped someone who was frustrated with technology.
points: The person's frustration and what was actually wrong
How you helped — patience, clear steps, follow-up
The outcome and what it taught you about users
pitfalls: Being condescending about their skill level
Fixing it without teaching anything

behavioral.prompt: Why are you pursuing a cybersecurity career, and what have you done in the last 90 days to prepare?
points: A genuine motivation — what draws you to this work
Concrete recent actions — study, labs, this course, projects
How those actions connect to entry-level security work
pitfalls: Generic answer anyone could give
No evidence of recent effort
